highlights.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-14422-750x422.png) ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models A team of urban resilience and earthquake engineering researchers has unveiled a complete pipeline for building large language models that can absorb the sprawling, fragmented knowledge of resilient cities and then deploy it across professional disaster-prevention tasks. The framework, called ResCity-LLM, links together four stages that had previously existed in isolation: assembling a domain corpus, generating training data automatically, adapting open-source models through a two-stage training strategy, and evaluating the results on a purpose-built benchmark. When the strongest adapted model was tested against two much larger general-purpose systems, it came out ahead on the benchmark’s overall weighted score, offering early evidence that compact, locally deployable models can compete with cloud giants in a specialized engineering domain. The motivation stems from an uncomfortable mismatch between what urban resilience research demands and what general-purpose language models are trained to do. Urban resilience draws on engineering, environment, planning, ecology, economics, sociology and governance simultaneously, with relevant knowledge scattered across academic papers, technical standards, planning documents, policy texts and case studies. General-purpose models such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Claude are trained overwhelmingly on general text, so they struggle to cover the complex knowledge structures, specialized semantics and typical task scenarios of this interdisciplinary field. Unlike medicine or law, where domain-specific language model research is relatively mature, resilience-oriented work had remained scattered and exploratory, lacking a systematic framework that spans corpus organization, training data construction, model training and specialized benchmark evaluation. The first ingredient is a data foundation the researchers call ResCity-Corpus. Using keywords related to urban and resilient cities in both English and Chinese, the team harvested academic literature from Elsevier, Nature, Springer, arXiv and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, crawled news reports from mainstream media platforms, and collected professional monographs together with national, industry and local technical standards covering disaster prevention, urban lifeline systems and related fields. The final processed corpus for continued pre-training contained 60,059 text blocks amounting to 96.80 million tokens, split roughly 69 percent English and 31 percent Chinese, and organized into seven thematic categories ranging from hazard and climate science to governance and public policy. Raw corpora of this kind are notoriously messy, so the researchers designed what they call a multi-agent collaborative dual-stage data generation pipeline. In the first stage, aimed at continued pre-training, a clean-agent parses heterogeneous documents and strips out noise, a chunk-agent segments long texts into semantically coherent units sized by tokenizer length with overlapping tails to preserve context, a quality-agent powered by a commercial language model scores each chunk and flags low-quality or incomplete samples, and a repair-agent performs minimal fixes to broken sentences and grammatical errors without altering the underlying knowledge content. highlights.content: UPDATED 20:55 EDT / OCTOBER 23 2026 ### Moonshot AI launches new flagship Kim K3.1 Pro model with 3T parameters Moonshot AI today introduced Kim K3.1 Pro, a large language model that can perform some tasks better than Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. The LLM is a post-trained, or upgraded, version of an algorithm that the Chinese artificial intelligence company released in July. The latter model, Kimi K3, comprises 896 individual neural networks with 3 trillion parameters. It only activates 16 of those neural networks at any given time to minimize inference costs. Moonshot AI also optimizes its models’ hardware footprint in other ways. Kim K3 features Kimi Delta Attention, a custom implementation of a memory-saving technology called Gated DeltaNet. It reduces the amount of RAM that the model’s attention mechanism uses to interpret user prompts. The feature was presumably carried over to Kim K3.1 Pro. The company says the new model’s post-training workflow consumed significantly more processing power than similar projects it completed in the past. Additionally, it ran on an upgraded version of the company’s post-training stack. Moonshot AI added automated quality checks and boosted the underlying infrastructure’s efficiency. One area where Kimi K3.1 Pro delivers particularly competitive output quality is 3D modeling. There are two ways to create a 3D model of an object: engineers can draw it or they can write a code snippet that specifies its geometry in numerical terms. Kimi K3.1 Pro takes the latter approach. The LLM scored 92.7% on a 3D model coding benchmark called BenchCAD, which put it within four percentage points of Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. Kimi K3.1 Pro can not only generate static 3D models but also animate them. In one test, Moonshot AI used the model to generate an animated simulation of human motion. Another internal evaluation saw the company create multiple 3D video games. Games are difficult for AI models to generate because they contain a large amount of code and even a single bug can crash them. Pro scored 65.7% on the industry standard Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding benchmark, which put it more than 7% ahead of Astra but slightly behind Opus 5.5. Furthermore, it managed to outperform both models on OfficeQA Pro v2. It’s a test that measures LLMs’ ability to perform complex financial analysis tasks. The model’s performance on popular cybersecurity benchmarks significantly trails the scores of Astra and Opus 5.5. According to Moonshot AI, its engineers deliberately removed cybersecurity-related information from the model’s post-training dataset to address safety risks. The company plans to equip its future models with more advanced vulnerability analysis features. Kimi K3.1 Pro is available via Moonshot AI’s paid cloud services on launch. highlights.content: ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)![](https://www.elektormagazine.com/waitress/takeaway/270/image) ![llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs](https://cdn.eenewseurope.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Copy-of-Copy-of-Article-Image-Template-2026-10-22T092241.444-scaled-800x600-c-default.png) # llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs News | By Glaucileine Vieira [open source](/en/tags/open-source/) [LLM](/en/tags/llm-2/) [AI](/en/tags/ai/) [Data Centers](/en/tags/data-centers-2/) --- Running large AI models is expensive, especially when thousands of requests compete for computing resources. The open-source llm-d project aims to tackle that problem with version 1.0, introducing new capabilities for managing [AI](https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/tags/ai) inference across distributed infrastructure. Founded by Red Hat, IBM, Google Cloud, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA, the project is now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). For *eeNews Europe* readers, the release is particularly relevant to companies developing AI infrastructure and deploying large language models. It offers ways to improve GPU utilization, manage demanding workloads, and reduce the cost of running AI applications. ## AI Inference Gets More Efficient One of the biggest challenges in AI inference is managing the information models need to process and reuse. This becomes especially demanding with AI agents, which often handle long conversations, access large amounts of context, and run multiple tasks simultaneously. llm-d addresses these challenges through techniques such as cache-aware routing, memory offloading, and separating the processing of input prompts from generating responses. Version 1.0 adds improved workload scheduling, allowing different users and applications to share computing resources without overwhelming the system. It also introduces high-availability routing and coordinated updates, helping operators maintain services during maintenance. ## Lower Costs on Existing GPUs Recent demonstrations show what these improvements could mean for large AI deployments. In one benchmark, researchers used llm-d to run GLM 5.2, an open-weight model with approximately 753 billion parameters, on NVIDIA GPUs. The system delivered more than 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak and supported up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents without preemptions. Based on current cloud rental rates, the researchers estimated inference costs five to ten times lower per token than comparable commercial API pricing for the tested workloads. Another project at IBM Research used open models and llm-d to investigate quantum error correction hardware. Researchers reported inference costs 11.5 times lower than an entirely proprietary configuration, with a cache hit rate of approximately 98%. These results come from specific workloads and configurations, rather than general performance guarantees. ## Built for Production AI Workloads Beyond performance, llm-d 1.0 focuses on making distributed AI inference easier to operate in production environments. The release introduces multi-tenant quality of service, session-aware routing, and support for updates without planned downtime. The full weights, model card and serving guidance landed on Hugging Face on July 27, 2026, eleven days after the July 16 launch. It is not the cheapest model here, the smallest, or the most permissively licensed. It is the one with the biggest documented ceiling. Four rivals make the best open source LLM question harder than any single leaderboard can settle. GLM-5.3 from Z.ai is the current flagship of a family that now stretches down to cheap Flash tiers. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, refreshed on October 17 as V4.1-Flash-1017, undercuts nearly everyone on price. Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 line pairs a hosted Max flagship with open checkpoints that differ by size and license. highlights.content: ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)![](https://www.elektormagazine.com/waitress/takeaway/270/image) ![llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs](https://cdn.eenewseurope.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Copy-of-Copy-of-Article-Image-Template-2026-10-22T092241.444-scaled-800x600-c-default.png) # llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs News | By Glaucileine Vieira [open source](/en/tags/open-source/) [LLM](/en/tags/llm-2/) [AI](/en/tags/ai/) [Data Centers](/en/tags/data-centers-2/) --- Running large AI models is expensive, especially when thousands of requests compete for computing resources. The open-source llm-d project aims to tackle that problem with version 1.0, introducing new capabilities for managing [AI](https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/tags/ai) inference across distributed infrastructure. Founded by Red Hat, IBM, Google Cloud, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA, the project is now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). For *eeNews Europe* readers, the release is particularly relevant to companies developing AI infrastructure and deploying large language models. It offers ways to improve GPU utilization, manage demanding workloads, and reduce the cost of running AI applications. ## AI Inference Gets More Efficient One of the biggest challenges in AI inference is managing the information models need to process and reuse. This becomes especially demanding with AI agents, which often handle long conversations, access large amounts of context, and run multiple tasks simultaneously. llm-d addresses these challenges through techniques such as cache-aware routing, memory offloading, and separating the processing of input prompts from generating responses. Version 1.0 adds improved workload scheduling, allowing different users and applications to share computing resources without overwhelming the system. It also introduces high-availability routing and coordinated updates, helping operators maintain services during maintenance. ## Lower Costs on Existing GPUs Recent demonstrations show what these improvements could mean for large AI deployments. In one benchmark, researchers used llm-d to run GLM 5.2, an open-weight model with approximately 753 billion parameters, on NVIDIA GPUs. The system delivered more than 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak and supported up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents without preemptions. Based on current cloud rental rates, the researchers estimated inference costs five to ten times lower per token than comparable commercial API pricing for the tested workloads. Another project at IBM Research used open models and llm-d to investigate quantum error correction hardware. Researchers reported inference costs 11.5 times lower than an entirely proprietary configuration, with a cache hit rate of approximately 98%. These results come from specific workloads and configurations, rather than general performance guarantees. ## Built for Production AI Workloads Beyond performance, llm-d 1.0 focuses on making distributed AI inference easier to operate in production environments. highlights.content: [![UC Today](/_next/image?url=%2Fbrand%2Fuc-today-logo.png&w=1920&q=75)powering productive workplaces](/) [Front page](/) News[Trust & Risk](/beat/trust-risk)15h · 09:01 BST · 4 min read # AI Agent Risks, Exchange Issues and a Shifting Cyber Market Microsoft is warning that autonomous AI agents could create insider threats, while October Windows updates are disrupting some Exchange Server environments and US cybersecurity job postings are falling despite sharp growth in demand for specialist AI security roles, highlighting the operational and ![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fjrueuulzybfnqbgsdwwt.supabase.co%2Fstorage%2Fv1%2Fobject%2Fpublic%2Favatars%2F3b8ec3f4-d7e8-43c3-9dc6-e95bb2de1c58%2Favatar.jfif%3Fv%3D1787131806280&w=3840&q=75)[Kristian McCann](/author/kristian-mccann) For a while now, AI agents have been a growing source of cybersecurity concern, but this week Microsoft has raised an uncomfortable question: what happens when the technology you're relying on to get work done becomes a security risk itself? The company is warning that agents don't need to be hacked or deliberately turned malicious to cause problems. That's not to say AI agents are suddenly running amok across businesses. Rather, Microsoft is concerned about how much freedom organizations are giving them, particularly when they can access sensitive data and make decisions without human approval. Its proposed solution is to use Guardian Agents to monitor their counterparts, adding another layer of oversight to increasingly autonomous systems. Elsewhere this week, Microsoft's October Windows updates are causing problems for Exchange Server deployments, with administrators reporting email disruption and database availability issues. At the same time, new cybersecurity jobs data points to a contracting market, even as demand for AI Security Engineers and Cyber Data Scientists rises sharply. These developments raise different questions about keeping critical business systems running and how cybersecurity skills demand is changing. ## Microsoft Warns AI Agents Could Become Insider Threats Microsoft is urging organizations to treat AI agents as potential insider threats, warning that systems with access to sensitive data and business-critical tools can cause harm without being deliberately compromised. The company published its latest guidance on October 19, arguing that security controls must account for agents that [behave unpredictably](https://uctoday.com/openai-just-went-rogue-and-cyber-attacked-a-startup) as their tasks and surrounding context change. **Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella** argues that organizations should separate a model's intelligence from its authority, saying: > “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.” In practice, that means the model should not control the security boundaries governing its own access or actions. As Nadella explained, the most trustworthy systems are those designed to operate within external constraints, rather than relying on confidence in the model itself. The company is proposing Guardian Agents to monitor other agents, assess changing risk and intervene when necessary. This builds on Project Perception, introduced in July, which combines enterprise security signals with specialized red, blue and green agents to identify weaknesses, investigate threats and help remediate problems. Microsoft is now extending that approach to the risks posed by agents operating inside organizations. ## Exchange Server Instability Follows October Windows Updates Microsoft has acknowledged reports that October's Windows Server updates are causing instability in some Exchange Server environments. highlights.content: [News](/news)[Fraud and Fincrime](/fraud-and-fincrime) # BBVA teams up with NVIDIA to explore AI agent security architecture ![Stefana Apetrei](https://assets.thepaypers.com/Team%20Folder/team-people-b.png) Stefana Apetrei 23 Oct 2026 / 5 Min Read BBVA has announced plans to work with NVIDIA on OpenShell, a reference architecture for AI agent safety, security, and governance. According to the statement, the initiative is part of the bank’s plan to scale AI agents across the organisation while keeping oversight and control over their activities. No timeline for deployment has been disclosed. ## Governing autonomous agents at runtime AI agents are taking on more complex tasks with greater autonomy. As a result, organisations need to define clear limits on what agents can do and keep control over how they operate. [NVIDIA’s OpenShell](https://thepaypers.com/fraud-and-fincrime/news/nvidia-introduces-open-agent-safety-platform-for-ai-agents) Reference Architecture is designed to address this through mechanisms that govern agent behaviour and intervene when established security boundaries are crossed. The architecture combines two elements. The first is infrastructure for running AI agents and managing their interactions with other tools. The second is a set of independent security systems that detect and contain actions exceeding set limits. This design rests on the premise that controls applied at the design stage are not sufficient on their own. Because agents carry out sequences of actions, from retrieving information to using external tools, securing them also depends on monitoring their decisions and actions during execution. The OpenShell secure runtime software is open source. The announcement builds on existing open-source AI safety initiatives that already involve companies across the technology stack, with BBVA being among them. ## Relevance for financial services Traceability and risk management are core requirements in financial services, which makes runtime governance of autonomous systems particularly relevant for banks. For BBVA, working with NVIDIA is a way to test approaches that build security and governance into agents from the design stage onwards. The work fits within the bank’s strategy to industrialise the development and deployment of AI systems across the group, which aims to improve customer experience and simplify internal processes. *Aser Blanco*, Global Banking Lead at *NVIDIA*, noted that banks using agents with their proprietary intelligence need clear boundaries and oversight at every stage as autonomy increases. Through the collaboration, Blanco added, BBVA will explore how to enforce those boundaries while agents are operating. The company is warning that agents don't need to be hacked or deliberately turned malicious to cause problems. That's not to say AI agents are suddenly running amok across businesses. Rather, Microsoft is concerned about how much freedom organizations are giving them, particularly when they can access sensitive data and make decisions without human approval. Its proposed solution is to use Guardian Agents to monitor their counterparts, adding another layer of oversight to increasingly autonomous systems. Elsewhere this week, Microsoft's October Windows updates are causing problems for Exchange Server deployments, with administrators reporting email disruption and database availability issues. At the same time, new cybersecurity jobs data points to a contracting market, even as demand for AI Security Engineers and Cyber Data Scientists rises sharply. These developments raise different questions about keeping critical business systems running and how cybersecurity skills demand is changing. ## Microsoft Warns AI Agents Could Become Insider Threats Microsoft is urging organizations to treat AI agents as potential insider threats, warning that systems with access to sensitive data and business-critical tools can cause harm without being deliberately compromised. The company published its latest guidance on October 19, arguing that security controls must account for agents that [behave unpredictably](https://uctoday.com/openai-just-went-rogue-and-cyber-attacked-a-startup) as their tasks and surrounding context change. **Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella** argues that organizations should separate a model's intelligence from its authority, saying: > “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.” In practice, that means the model should not control the security boundaries governing its own access or actions. As Nadella explained, the most trustworthy systems are those designed to operate within external constraints, rather than relying on confidence in the model itself. The company is proposing Guardian Agents to monitor other agents, assess changing risk and intervene when necessary. This builds on Project Perception, introduced in July, which combines enterprise security signals with specialized red, blue and green agents to identify weaknesses, investigate threats and help remediate problems. Microsoft is now extending that approach to the risks posed by agents operating inside organizations. ## Exchange Server Instability Follows October Windows Updates Microsoft has acknowledged reports that October's Windows Server updates are causing instability in some Exchange Server environments. No timeline for deployment has been disclosed. ## Governing autonomous agents at runtime AI agents are taking on more complex tasks with greater autonomy. As a result, organisations need to define clear limits on what agents can do and keep control over how they operate. [NVIDIA’s OpenShell](https://thepaypers.com/fraud-and-fincrime/news/nvidia-introduces-open-agent-safety-platform-for-ai-agents) Reference Architecture is designed to address this through mechanisms that govern agent behaviour and intervene when established security boundaries are crossed. The architecture combines two elements. The first is infrastructure for running AI agents and managing their interactions with other tools. The second is a set of independent security systems that detect and contain actions exceeding set limits. This design rests on the premise that controls applied at the design stage are not sufficient on their own. Because agents carry out sequences of actions, from retrieving information to using external tools, securing them also depends on monitoring their decisions and actions during execution. The OpenShell secure runtime software is open source. The announcement builds on existing open-source AI safety initiatives that already involve companies across the technology stack, with BBVA being among them. ## Relevance for financial services Traceability and risk management are core requirements in financial services, which makes runtime governance of autonomous systems particularly relevant for banks. For BBVA, working with NVIDIA is a way to test approaches that build security and governance into agents from the design stage onwards. The work fits within the bank’s strategy to industrialise the development and deployment of AI systems across the group, which aims to improve customer experience and simplify internal processes. *Aser Blanco*, Global Banking Lead at *NVIDIA*, noted that banks using agents with their proprietary intelligence need clear boundaries and oversight at every stage as autonomy increases. Through the collaboration, Blanco added, BBVA will explore how to enforce those boundaries while agents are operating. This supports the bank’s goals for customer experience and employee productivity without giving up control. AI Agents.content: # You gave your AI agent access, but who is giving it orders? ###### Gen Digital * October 23, 2026 * 10:00 AM * 0 Headlines warn that AI could threaten humanity, and it’s easy to wave that off as science fiction. But the real danger is more ordinary and already here. Research published by Gen Threat Labs demonstrated how quickly an AI agent’s autonomy can become a liability. In a controlled experiment, researchers manipulated an agent through content it encountered while reading email, prompting it to execute system commands, transmit data outside its environment and perform destructive file operations. No software vulnerability was required. The agent simply treated untrusted content as instruction. That autonomy is expanding daily. Agents are moving from answering questions to taking action doing everything from executing code, connecting to services, managing files and making decisions on a user’s behalf. The shift from developer-focused tools like OpenClaw to widespread use of personal assistants like Muse, happened quickly. Delegating work across platforms is becoming commonplace and how people interact with AI. The risks extend beyond manipulating agents. In October, Gen Threat Labs documented Warden Stealer, malware targeting configuration files and local data associated with AI assistants and coding tools, potentially exposing credentials, access tokens and conversation histories. When software can act with a user’s permissions, trust can’t be reduced to whether a model produces a safe-sounding answer. People need to know what an agent can access, where it is connecting, what it is doing and whether the protection around it works. That is why Gen is building the Agent Trust Hub: a trust layer designed to extend protection across the agent lifecycle, from verification and visibility to runtime safety and enforcement. ## Trust starts before an agent acts Agentic systems gain capabilities through skills, plugins, tools and other integrations. These extensions make agents more useful, but they also expand risk by introducing hidden instructions, excessive permissions, and malicious code. Earlier this year, Gen researchers identified that 12% of skills available on ClawHub – at the time – were malicious. Many impersonated legitimate extensions while introducing instructions designed to trick agents into downloading malware. The Agent Trust Hub (ATH) helps assess these risks before a capability is installed or used. It brings together skill scanning, a curated marketplace of trusted skills and mechanisms that allow agents to check themselves for safety. Gen’s partnership with Vercel also brings verification and visible risk ratings into the skills.sh ecosystem, where developers discover and install new capabilities. ## Securing how agents connect Agents communicate across services, regions and websites, often at a speed and scale that traditional human-oriented controls were not designed to manage. VPN for Agents, a part of the ATH, addresses that connectivity gap with an AI-native VPN built for autonomous agents. Powered by Norton VPN infrastructure, it provides encrypted, private connectivity without requiring a conventional client installation. Its multi-tunnel design allows multiple agents to operate simultaneously through separate protected connections, including across different countries. The architecture gives people greater control over how agents communicate and helps protect an agent’s identity and location while it works. ## Use AI Agents Safely with Gen's Agent Trust Hub AI agents can install skills and take action on your behalf, which makes a single compromised skill a security risk. LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-14422-750x422.png) ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models A team of urban resilience and earthquake engineering researchers has unveiled a complete pipeline for building large language models that can absorb the sprawling, fragmented knowledge of resilient cities and then deploy it across professional disaster-prevention tasks. The framework, called ResCity-LLM, links together four stages that had previously existed in isolation: assembling a domain corpus, generating training data automatically, adapting open-source models through a two-stage training strategy, and evaluating the results on a purpose-built benchmark. When the strongest adapted model was tested against two much larger general-purpose systems, it came out ahead on the benchmark’s overall weighted score, offering early evidence that compact, locally deployable models can compete with cloud giants in a specialized engineering domain. The motivation stems from an uncomfortable mismatch between what urban resilience research demands and what general-purpose language models are trained to do. Urban resilience draws on engineering, environment, planning, ecology, economics, sociology and governance simultaneously, with relevant knowledge scattered across academic papers, technical standards, planning documents, policy texts and case studies. General-purpose models such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Claude are trained overwhelmingly on general text, so they struggle to cover the complex knowledge structures, specialized semantics and typical task scenarios of this interdisciplinary field. Unlike medicine or law, where domain-specific language model research is relatively mature, resilience-oriented work had remained scattered and exploratory, lacking a systematic framework that spans corpus organization, training data construction, model training and specialized benchmark evaluation. The first ingredient is a data foundation the researchers call ResCity-Corpus. Using keywords related to urban and resilient cities in both English and Chinese, the team harvested academic literature from Elsevier, Nature, Springer, arXiv and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, crawled news reports from mainstream media platforms, and collected professional monographs together with national, industry and local technical standards covering disaster prevention, urban lifeline systems and related fields. The final processed corpus for continued pre-training contained 60,059 text blocks amounting to 96.80 million tokens, split roughly 69 percent English and 31 percent Chinese, and organized into seven thematic categories ranging from hazard and climate science to governance and public policy. Raw corpora of this kind are notoriously messy, so the researchers designed what they call a multi-agent collaborative dual-stage data generation pipeline. In the first stage, aimed at continued pre-training, a clean-agent parses heterogeneous documents and strips out noise, a chunk-agent segments long texts into semantically coherent units sized by tokenizer length with overlapping tails to preserve context, a quality-agent powered by a commercial language model scores each chunk and flags low-quality or incomplete samples, and a repair-agent performs minimal fixes to broken sentences and grammatical errors without altering the underlying knowledge content. LLMs.content: UPDATED 20:55 EDT / OCTOBER 23 2026 ### Moonshot AI launches new flagship Kim K3.1 Pro model with 3T parameters Moonshot AI today introduced Kim K3.1 Pro, a large language model that can perform some tasks better than Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. The LLM is a post-trained, or upgraded, version of an algorithm that the Chinese artificial intelligence company released in July. The latter model, Kimi K3, comprises 896 individual neural networks with 3 trillion parameters. It only activates 16 of those neural networks at any given time to minimize inference costs. Moonshot AI also optimizes its models’ hardware footprint in other ways. Kim K3 features Kimi Delta Attention, a custom implementation of a memory-saving technology called Gated DeltaNet. It reduces the amount of RAM that the model’s attention mechanism uses to interpret user prompts. The feature was presumably carried over to Kim K3.1 Pro. The company says the new model’s post-training workflow consumed significantly more processing power than similar projects it completed in the past. Additionally, it ran on an upgraded version of the company’s post-training stack. Moonshot AI added automated quality checks and boosted the underlying infrastructure’s efficiency. One area where Kimi K3.1 Pro delivers particularly competitive output quality is 3D modeling. There are two ways to create a 3D model of an object: engineers can draw it or they can write a code snippet that specifies its geometry in numerical terms. Kimi K3.1 Pro takes the latter approach. The LLM scored 92.7% on a 3D model coding benchmark called BenchCAD, which put it within four percentage points of Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. Kimi K3.1 Pro can not only generate static 3D models but also animate them. In one test, Moonshot AI used the model to generate an animated simulation of human motion. Another internal evaluation saw the company create multiple 3D video games. Games are difficult for AI models to generate because they contain a large amount of code and even a single bug can crash them. Pro scored 65.7% on the industry standard Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding benchmark, which put it more than 7% ahead of Astra but slightly behind Opus 5.5. Furthermore, it managed to outperform both models on OfficeQA Pro v2. It’s a test that measures LLMs’ ability to perform complex financial analysis tasks. The model’s performance on popular cybersecurity benchmarks significantly trails the scores of Astra and Opus 5.5. According to Moonshot AI, its engineers deliberately removed cybersecurity-related information from the model’s post-training dataset to address safety risks. The company plans to equip its future models with more advanced vulnerability analysis features. Kimi K3.1 Pro is available via Moonshot AI’s paid cloud services on launch. LLMs.content: ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)![](https://www.elektormagazine.com/waitress/takeaway/270/image) ![llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs](https://cdn.eenewseurope.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Copy-of-Copy-of-Article-Image-Template-2026-10-22T092241.444-scaled-800x600-c-default.png) # llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs News | By Glaucileine Vieira [open source](/en/tags/open-source/) [LLM](/en/tags/llm-2/) [AI](/en/tags/ai/) [Data Centers](/en/tags/data-centers-2/) --- Running large AI models is expensive, especially when thousands of requests compete for computing resources. The open-source llm-d project aims to tackle that problem with version 1.0, introducing new capabilities for managing [AI](https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/tags/ai) inference across distributed infrastructure. Founded by Red Hat, IBM, Google Cloud, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA, the project is now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). For *eeNews Europe* readers, the release is particularly relevant to companies developing AI infrastructure and deploying large language models. It offers ways to improve GPU utilization, manage demanding workloads, and reduce the cost of running AI applications. ## AI Inference Gets More Efficient One of the biggest challenges in AI inference is managing the information models need to process and reuse. This becomes especially demanding with AI agents, which often handle long conversations, access large amounts of context, and run multiple tasks simultaneously. llm-d addresses these challenges through techniques such as cache-aware routing, memory offloading, and separating the processing of input prompts from generating responses. Version 1.0 adds improved workload scheduling, allowing different users and applications to share computing resources without overwhelming the system. It also introduces high-availability routing and coordinated updates, helping operators maintain services during maintenance. ## Lower Costs on Existing GPUs Recent demonstrations show what these improvements could mean for large AI deployments. In one benchmark, researchers used llm-d to run GLM 5.2, an open-weight model with approximately 753 billion parameters, on NVIDIA GPUs. The system delivered more than 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak and supported up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents without preemptions. Based on current cloud rental rates, the researchers estimated inference costs five to ten times lower per token than comparable commercial API pricing for the tested workloads. Another project at IBM Research used open models and llm-d to investigate quantum error correction hardware. Researchers reported inference costs 11.5 times lower than an entirely proprietary configuration, with a cache hit rate of approximately 98%. These results come from specific workloads and configurations, rather than general performance guarantees. ## Built for Production AI Workloads Beyond performance, llm-d 1.0 focuses on making distributed AI inference easier to operate in production environments. The release introduces multi-tenant quality of service, session-aware routing, and support for updates without planned downtime. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Best Open Source LLM in October 2026: The Short Answer Kimi K3 is the strongest open-weight model you can download today, judging by what Moonshot AI has published: a [2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts design with native vision and a 1-million-token context window](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k3-quickstart). The full weights, model card and serving guidance landed on Hugging Face on July 27, 2026, eleven days after the July 16 launch. It is not the cheapest model here, the smallest, or the most permissively licensed. It is the one with the biggest documented ceiling. Four rivals make the best open source LLM question harder than any single leaderboard can settle. GLM-5.3 from Z.ai is the current flagship of a family that now stretches down to cheap Flash tiers. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, refreshed on October 17 as V4.1-Flash-1017, undercuts nearly everyone on price. Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 line pairs a hosted Max flagship with open checkpoints that differ by size and license. Mistral Large 4 sits in public preview, with weights promised by the end of October but not downloadable on October 23. The field moves weekly. [Kimi K3’s run on a coding leaderboard](https://shattered.io/kimi-k3-coding-leaderboard-2026/) earlier this month put Chinese open-weight labs in the spotlight, and a stream of releases since then has crowded the shortlist. Specs, license terms, published benchmarks, per-token prices, hardware needs and migration effort all point in slightly different directions, so the right winner depends on what you plan to build. ### Quick picks by priority * **Highest documented ceiling:** Kimi K3, with open weights, 2.8T parameters and a 1M-token window. * **Lowest price per token:** DeepSeek V4.1-Flash at $0.15 input and $0.60 output off-peak, with GLM-5.3-Flash close behind at $0.15 input and $0.50 output. * **Best fit for one workstation GPU:** the Qwen3.8 27B dense checkpoint, which secondary reports tie to an Apache 2.0 license. * **Best for agentic coding and security work:** GLM-5.3, based on Z.ai’s own claims. * **Best bet for European data residency:** Mistral Large 4, once its weights and license actually ship. ### What is confirmed and what is not Treat every vendor-reported benchmark as a claim until an independent leaderboard repeats it. No head-to-head test covering all five models existed on October 23, 2026, and several of the numbers below come from the labs themselves. Where a figure rests on one report, the wording says “reportedly” or names the outlet. Where a successor is announced but unreleased, such as DeepSeek V4.1-Pro or Alibaba’s Qwen 4, it gets one sentence and no invented dates. ## Open Source vs Open Weight: What Each License Really Allows Almost none of the models people call open source LLMs meet the strict definition. You get the trained weights and usually a model card, but not the training data, the full training code or the right to do anything you like. Open weight is the accurate label, and the license attached to those weights decides whether a startup, a bank or a government contractor can ship a product on top of them. Kimi K3 shows the pattern clearly. Moonshot published the weights under a custom Kimi K3 License, and coverage of the release is explicit that it should not be described as MIT or Apache 2.0. An inner loop implements each candidate, checks it for correctness, and benchmarks it against the target workload. LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Riemann’s 13.1B-Parameter AI Model Hits Hugging Face [2026] ![Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/mbell.webp) [Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/author/mbell/) Updated Oct 23, 2026 · 15 min read Riemann Computing Inc. published a prerelease of a 13B parameter AI model on October 21, 2026, and says the training method behind it points toward lower model training costs. The model, named **My Name Is Riemann**, carries 13,110,702,080 parameters and sits on the Hugging Face Model Hub under the OpenPeerAI organization. A company press release distributed through EIN Presswire and carried by the Akron Beacon Journal’s press-release section put the announcement into circulation that evening. The details that are checkable look solid. The architecture, file sizes, token counts and training dates all appear in the public repository. The pitch is another matter. The company has not published a dollar figure, a GPU-hour count or a benchmark table, so the headline claim about cheaper training stays an assertion for now. This analysis separates what Riemann Computing has documented from what it has only promised. The release lands in a crowded month for open weights. Our [ranking of five open-source LLMs from $0.15 input](https://shattered.io/best-open-source-llm-october-2026-kimi-glm-deepseek/) shows how fast the mid-size field moves, and a prerelease from a small lab has to be read against that backdrop. Below, we walk through the spec sheet, the training record, the cost argument, the competitive picture and five predictions. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Riemann Computing Announced on October 21 The announcement is short on drama and long on specifics about the artifact. Riemann Computing Inc. says it created a prerelease version of a 13B model and demonstrated it publicly. The new [SpaceX Super Intelligence Partner Network](https://x.ai/partners) is open to “transformation partners” that help businesses deploy the Grok platform and to “marketplace partners” that build plugins and integrations that connect Grok to other tools, the release said. The SpaceX Super Intelligence Partner Network has more than 130 launch partners, including [Bain & Company](https://www.bain.com/), [Databricks](https://www.databricks.com/home-overview), [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/) and [Snowflake](https://www.snowflake.com/en/), per the release. ![Preferred Source](https://www.pymnts.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Google-PYMNTS-blackbox.svg) We’d love to be your [preferred source for news](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=pymnts.com). Grok Bot reached 418,000 weekly users as of Sept. 14, up 24% from the previous week, according to the report. Grok Bot, which was introduced in mid-August, is positioned as an enterprise product and is designed to handle workplace tasks, such as responding to emails, updating sales databases, processing invoices, organizing work and filing software bugs, per the report. AI Product.titleZh: StorageChain Launches Atlas, Its Native Enterprise LLM - 'Keep Your Data Out of Big AI'
AI Product.content: [![AiThority](https://aithority.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/AIT_1-1.png)](https://aithority.com/) Artificial Intelligence | News | Insights | AiThority [![AiThority](https://aithority.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/AIT_1-1.png) AiThority - Artificial Intelligence | News | Insights | AiThority](https://aithority.com/) [![AiThority](https://aithority.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/AIT_1-1.png)](https://aithority.com/) # StorageChain Launches Atlas, Its Native Enterprise LLM – ‘Keep Your Data Out of Big AI’ [Machine Learning](https://aithority.com/category/machine-learning/)[News](https://aithority.com/category/news/) [![](https://aithority.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/ein-150x72.png)By **EIN Presswire**](https://aithority.com/author/ein-presswire/ "Browse Author Articles") **Share** #### ***New proprietary model gives businesses a private, industry-focused AI option while reducing reliance on costly per-seat third-party AI subscriptions.*** [StorageChain](https://storagechain.io/) LLC, developer of the StorageChain AI Connect enterprise AI connectivity and intelligence platform, today announced Atlas, its proprietary enterprise large language model designed to let organizations search, analyze and interact with their own company data and knowledge base without sending sensitive enterprise data to major third-party AI providers. https://storagechain.io/atlas > Atlas changes the enterprise AI equation: keep control of your data, avoid unnecessary per-seat costs, and choose the AI model that works for your business.” > > — Chris Dominguez The launch marks a major expansion of StorageChain’s platform and its evolution into a native AI company. With Atlas, StorageChain now combines its permission-aware enterprise data connectivity layer with its own LLM, while continuing to give customers the option to connect to leading external models such as ChatGPT and other AI platforms. **Also Read: [AiThority Interview with Gou Rao, co-founder and CEO at NeuBird AI](https://aithority.com/interviews/aithority-interview-with-gou-rao-co-founder-and-ceo-at-neubird-ai/)** The result is choice. Organizations seeking maximum privacy and control can use Atlas without giving their business data to Big AI. Customers that prefer third-party models can continue to use them through StorageChain AI Connect. Companies can keep control of their data and make it AI-ready using StorageChain’s hosted or self-hosted model. Companies retain 100% control of their own data. Atlas gives customers access to full AI functionality without exposing data or paying expensive per seat licenses”. Atlas also introduces a different economic model for enterprise AI. Rather than requiring companies to purchase separate AI subscriptions for large numbers of employees, StorageChain is designed around the enterprise data being indexed and used. The agents help diagnose database issues, CPU spikes, and legacy automation while retaining human control. Control-M updates add workflow-level data validation, natural-language troubleshooting, and integrations including Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and LangGraph. Open Source AI.titleZh: llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs ...
Open Source AI.content: ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)![](https://www.elektormagazine.com/waitress/takeaway/270/image) ![llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs](https://cdn.eenewseurope.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Copy-of-Copy-of-Article-Image-Template-2026-10-22T092241.444-scaled-800x600-c-default.png) # llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs News | By Glaucileine Vieira [open source](/en/tags/open-source/) [LLM](/en/tags/llm-2/) [AI](/en/tags/ai/) [Data Centers](/en/tags/data-centers-2/) --- Running large AI models is expensive, especially when thousands of requests compete for computing resources. The open-source llm-d project aims to tackle that problem with version 1.0, introducing new capabilities for managing [AI](https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/tags/ai) inference across distributed infrastructure. Founded by Red Hat, IBM, Google Cloud, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA, the project is now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). For *eeNews Europe* readers, the release is particularly relevant to companies developing AI infrastructure and deploying large language models. It offers ways to improve GPU utilization, manage demanding workloads, and reduce the cost of running AI applications. ## AI Inference Gets More Efficient One of the biggest challenges in AI inference is managing the information models need to process and reuse. This becomes especially demanding with AI agents, which often handle long conversations, access large amounts of context, and run multiple tasks simultaneously. llm-d addresses these challenges through techniques such as cache-aware routing, memory offloading, and separating the processing of input prompts from generating responses. Version 1.0 adds improved workload scheduling, allowing different users and applications to share computing resources without overwhelming the system. It also introduces high-availability routing and coordinated updates, helping operators maintain services during maintenance. ## Lower Costs on Existing GPUs Recent demonstrations show what these improvements could mean for large AI deployments. In one benchmark, researchers used llm-d to run GLM 5.2, an open-weight model with approximately 753 billion parameters, on NVIDIA GPUs. The system delivered more than 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak and supported up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents without preemptions. Based on current cloud rental rates, the researchers estimated inference costs five to ten times lower per token than comparable commercial API pricing for the tested workloads. Another project at IBM Research used open models and llm-d to investigate quantum error correction hardware. Researchers reported inference costs 11.5 times lower than an entirely proprietary configuration, with a cache hit rate of approximately 98%. These results come from specific workloads and configurations, rather than general performance guarantees. ## Built for Production AI Workloads Beyond performance, llm-d 1.0 focuses on making distributed AI inference easier to operate in production environments. The release introduces multi-tenant quality of service, session-aware routing, and support for updates without planned downtime. The project now includes more than 500 contributors from over 25 organizations. “As organizations move beyond AI experimentation and into full-scale production, the bottleneck shifts from generating answers to managing the economics, operational reliability, and extreme infrastructure demands of complex agentic workloads,” said Brian Stevens, senior vice president and AI chief technology officer at ...

[Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Best Open Source LLM in October 2026: The Short Answer Kimi K3 is the strongest open-weight model you can download today, judging by what Moonshot AI has published: a [2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts design with native vision and a 1-million-token context window](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k3-quickstart). The full weights, model card and serving guidance landed on Hugging Face on July 27, 2026, eleven days after the July 16 launch. It is not the cheapest model here, the smallest, or the most permissively licensed. It is the one with the biggest documented ceiling. Four rivals make the best open source LLM question harder than any single leaderboard can settle. GLM-5.3 from Z.ai is the current flagship of a family that now stretches down to cheap Flash tiers. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, refreshed on October 17 as V4.1-Flash-1017, undercuts nearly everyone on price. Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 line pairs a hosted Max flagship with open checkpoints that differ by size and license. Mistral Large 4 sits in public preview, with weights promised by the end of October but not downloadable on October 23. The field moves weekly. [Kimi K3’s run on a coding leaderboard](https://shattered.io/kimi-k3-coding-leaderboard-2026/) earlier this month put Chinese open-weight labs in the spotlight, and a stream of releases since then has crowded the shortlist. Specs, license terms, published benchmarks, per-token prices, hardware needs and migration effort all point in slightly different directions, so the right winner depends on what you plan to build. ### Quick picks by priority * **Highest documented ceiling:** Kimi K3, with open weights, 2.8T parameters and a 1M-token window. * **Lowest price per token:** DeepSeek V4.1-Flash at $0.15 input and $0.60 output off-peak, with GLM-5.3-Flash close behind at $0.15 input and $0.50 output. * **Best fit for one workstation GPU:** the Qwen3.8 27B dense checkpoint, which secondary reports tie to an Apache 2.0 license. * **Best for agentic coding and security work:** GLM-5.3, based on Z.ai’s own claims. * **Best bet for European data residency:** Mistral Large 4, once its weights and license actually ship. ### What is confirmed and what is not Treat every vendor-reported benchmark as a claim until an independent leaderboard repeats it. No head-to-head test covering all five models existed on October 23, 2026, and several of the numbers below come from the labs themselves. Where a figure rests on one report, the wording says “reportedly” or names the outlet. Where a successor is announced but unreleased, such as DeepSeek V4.1-Pro or Alibaba’s Qwen 4, it gets one sentence and no invented dates. ## Open Source vs Open Weight: What Each License Really Allows Almost none of the models people call open source LLMs meet the strict definition. You get the trained weights and usually a model card, but not the training data, the full training code or the right to do anything you like. Open weight is the accurate label, and the license attached to those weights decides whether a startup, a bank or a government contractor can ship a product on top of them. Kimi K3 shows the pattern clearly. Moonshot published the weights under a custom Kimi K3 License, and coverage of the release is explicit that it should not be described as MIT or Apache 2.0. Open Source AI.title: LiteLLM says hackers poisoned it with GitHub tokens leaked via Claude Code
Open Source AI.titleZh: LiteLLM says hackers poisoned it with GitHub tokens leaked via Claude Code
Open Source AI.content: LiteLLM says hackers took the keys they needed from its own logs. They used them to publish a poisoned version of its software on Wednesday. The open-source AI gateway explained it in an incident report. Its chief executive, chief technology officer and director of security signed it. Its engineers found that Anthropic’s coding agent, Claude Code, sometimes puts a user’s GitHub command-line login token into a response. If something logs those responses, the tokens may end up in LiteLLM’s logs, the company said. > “We believe the attacker gained access to this deployment, obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from its logs, and subsequently used those credentials to compromise our release workflow,” LiteLLM wrote. The deployment was LiteLLM’s own internal one, open to the public internet. It held an “unexpected, innocuously named user account”, the company said. LiteLLM has not confirmed how the attacker got in, but suspects a recently patched vulnerability. ## Three stolen tokens LiteLLM lets developers reach many AI models through one API. The poisoned version, 1.107.0, sat on PyPI from 11:39 to 13:23 UTC on 21 October. PyPI is the main Python package index. Its Docker images were live from 11:46 to 14:20 UTC. LiteLLM said its official 1.107.0 source tag on GitHub does not contain the malicious files. Researchers at Upwind first reported the poisoned release on GitHub. LiteLLM said on X that it learned of it at 6:32am Pacific time. That was almost two hours after the release went out. The attacker held three developers’ GitHub credentials. On Monday, LiteLLM had widened release rights so two engineers could ship daily fixes for customers. The attacker used a token from one of its two GitHub organisation owners to switch off branch protection. A second developer’s credential approved the production release, which was built from a lookalike repository, Berri-AI/litellm. A third deleted the workflow records. ## Stolen keys put to use The package carried a credential stealer and a backdoor, according to the security firm Wiz. Both were set to run when Python starts. The stealer took browser passwords and cookies, cloud keys, SSH keys and API keys for AI services. It also pulled the AI provider keys stored in a LiteLLM proxy’s database. The backdoor works only on Linux and macOS. Every hour, it checked a GitHub repository for a server to fetch more code from. That repository never held more than test values, and GitHub took it down, Wiz said. It added that the malware showed strong signs of being written with AI help. Wiz cited data from ClickPy showing about 49,000 downloads of the poisoned version. About four and a half hours after the theft, Wiz saw the attacker test stolen Amazon Web Services credentials. They came from build servers and Kubernetes nodes. The checks included listing models on Amazon Bedrock. Wiz said this was consistent with LLMjacking, the use of stolen cloud access to run AI models. > “The dual-technique approach, using both .pth files and sitecustomize.py simultaneously, appears to be the first documented case in the wild,” Wiz researchers Benjamin Read and Rami McCarthy wrote. The attack landed on the same day as two critical PHP flaws. ## A second attack this year It is LiteLLM’s second compromise in 2026. In March, two poisoned versions sat on PyPI for about 40 minutes. LiteLLM traced that attack to Trivy, a security scanner in its build pipeline. Hackers also used Trivy to breach the European Commission. Mercor, an AI data firm, was hit too, and Meta froze AI data work with the company. Socket, a supply-chain security firm, told The Hacker News it had found no evidence linking the two attacks. It said the encryption keys, the way data was sent out and the backdoor all differ. > “That doesn’t rule out the same operator using different tooling, but we don’t have evidence to support that attribution,” Socket said. Open Source AI.title: ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI
Open Source AI.titleZh: ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI
Open Source AI.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-14422-750x422.png) ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models A team of urban resilience and earthquake engineering researchers has unveiled a complete pipeline for building large language models that can absorb the sprawling, fragmented knowledge of resilient cities and then deploy it across professional disaster-prevention tasks. The framework, called ResCity-LLM, links together four stages that had previously existed in isolation: assembling a domain corpus, generating training data automatically, adapting open-source models through a two-stage training strategy, and evaluating the results on a purpose-built benchmark. When the strongest adapted model was tested against two much larger general-purpose systems, it came out ahead on the benchmark’s overall weighted score, offering early evidence that compact, locally deployable models can compete with cloud giants in a specialized engineering domain. The motivation stems from an uncomfortable mismatch between what urban resilience research demands and what general-purpose language models are trained to do. Urban resilience draws on engineering, environment, planning, ecology, economics, sociology and governance simultaneously, with relevant knowledge scattered across academic papers, technical standards, planning documents, policy texts and case studies. General-purpose models such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Claude are trained overwhelmingly on general text, so they struggle to cover the complex knowledge structures, specialized semantics and typical task scenarios of this interdisciplinary field. Infra & Chips.content: ![](https://www.techtarget.com/rms/onlineimages/ai_a264431831_searchsitetablet_520X173.jpg) your123 - stock.adobe.com # AI inference is changing data center design requirements ## AI inference requires distinct infrastructure compared to training, focusing on low latency, appropriate hardware based on workload, and tailored power and cooling methods. ![Abhishek Jadhav](https://cdn.ttgtmedia.com/rms/onlineimages/abhishek_jadhav.jpg) Much of the current expansion of AI infrastructure has focused on large GPU clusters designed to train foundation models. These deployments concentrate substantial computing resources and require high-speed interconnects, electrical capacity and advanced cooling infrastructure. But as AI applications move into production, inference introduces different [infrastructure requirements](https://www.techtarget.com/ai/tip/Planning-AI-infrastructure-upgrades-Four-steps-for-success). Inference uses trained models to process requests for enterprise assistants, customer service, document processing and automated workflows. These workloads can vary in computing hardware, response-time requirements, geographic location, demand patterns and rack density. Infrastructure designed for large training clusters will not always be the most economical or appropriate option for every inference deployment. Data center operators and infrastructure leaders need to reassess how they design facilities and plan capacity to accommodate these different workload requirements. ## How inference workloads influence hardware selection Large-scale AI training relies on continuous computational throughput and high-speed communication among AI accelerators. However, inference has different infrastructure requirements because it must process incoming requests with low latency. Smaller models and some enterprise applications can run on CPUs. These processors support preprocessing, request handling and application orchestration. By contrast, larger generative models require GPUs for their parallel processing capabilities and high memory bandwidth. Factors such as model size, memory requirements and the number of simultaneous requests determine how much computing capacity an application requires. For example, a classification system that processes infrequent requests does not require the same infrastructure as a large language model ([LLM](https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/large-language-model-LLM)). However, some high-volume inferences can still require substantial accelerator capacity. For infrastructure teams, the starting point is the application's expected traffic, response time targets and processing requirements. These factors help determine if conventional servers, accelerator-equipped systems or larger GPU clusters are the right choice. ## Preparing power and cooling for AI inference Rack power density is the electrical load concentrated in a cabinet. More operators are reporting peak rack densities of 30 kW or higher, according to Uptime Institute's 2026 [survey](https://intelligence.uptimeinstitute.com/resource/uptime-institute-global-data-center-survey-2026). Nvidia's [GB200 NVL72](https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgxgb200-user-guide/hardware.html) rack consumes approximately 120 kW at full load, which shows why operators cannot use average facility rack densities to size every inference deployment. They need to analyze the electrical distribution at the rack, row and facility levels. Inference demand varies with application traffic and concurrent requests. Capacity planning should therefore account for peak loads, electrical headroom and potential [future expansion](https://www.techtarget.com/it-infrastructure/tip/Composable-architecture-Future-proofing-AI-expansion). Operators should avoid relying solely on average utilization as a metric. This platform aims to reduce water consumption for cooling by up to 100 per cent and generate the same AI output with up to 30 per cent less power. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 23, 2026 at 07:50 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Nvidia DSX platform helps European partners build AI factories with reduced water and power consumption. * DSX enables up to 100 per cent reduction in water use for cooling via dry-cooler-based heat rejection. * Dynamic power allocation with DSX MaxLPS can generate same AI output with up to 30 per cent less power. * DSX Flex allows AI factories to adapt workload power consumption to grid conditions and energy prices. Nvidia announced that its DSX AI Factory Platform is being adopted by European ecosystem partners to build [AI factories](/tag/ai+factories). The platform helps minimise water consumption for cooling and uses less power for the same AI output, according to the company. DSX also aids partners in bringing new capacity online faster and adapting workload power consumption to support grid reliability. DSX is a full-stack AI factory reference architecture, co-innovated with infrastructure companies. Compute, networking, storage, software, power, and cooling are codesigned as one system. ### Cooling and Power Efficiency [Nvidia DSX](/tag/nvidia+dsx) reference designs connect liquid-cooled computing with dry-cooler-based heat rejection. This approach avoids water evaporation for cooling. Nvidia Vera Rubin infrastructure supports 100 per cent [liquid cooling](/tag/liquid+cooling) with coolant temperatures up to 45 degrees Celsius. With dry-cooler-based designs, this architecture can reduce facility cooling water consumption to near zero. At a 2GW scale, Nvidia DSX can save 54 million litres of water daily compared with conventional cooling-tower systems. DSX MaxLPS dynamically allocates power within an AI factory’s budget. This helps operators generate the same tokens with up to 30 per cent less power. Operators can also support more GPU capacity within existing power budgets. DSX Flex assists AI factories in becoming flexible assets for the power grid. It enables operators to adapt workload power consumption to utility needs, demand-response events, and energy prices. This also coordinates electricity from the grid, onsite renewables, and energy storage. In Iceland, Nscale achieved 49 per cent higher inference throughput and 37 per cent more managed GPU capacity within the same 264-kilowatt power budget. Josh Payne, Founder and CEO of Nscale, stated that [Europe](/tag/europe)’s AI ambitions require making every megawatt count. He added that with Nvidia DSX, Nscale is building AI factories that deliver more compute from available power. ### Accelerating Design and Operations Nscale uses DSX Sim for its facilities in Portugal and Iceland to create [digital twins](/tag/digital+twins). Infra & Chips.content: * Energy & Engineering Group: [![Power Magazine](https://www.powermag.com/wp-content/themes/powermag-2025/assets/images/power-logo.svg)](https://www.powermag.com "PowerMag Home") Search --- ##### Sign In [Home](https://www.powermag.com/) [Data Centers](https://www.powermag.com/category/data-centers/) Why Flat Performance Matters More Than Peak Efficiency in Data Center Design [Data Centers](https://www.powermag.com/category/data-centers/ "Data Centers archive") # Why Flat Performance Matters More Than Peak Efficiency in Data Center Design Philip Zuk ![Why Flat Performance Matters More Than Peak Efficiency in Data Center Design](https://www.powermag.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/server-room-data-center-networking-database-co-2026-01-09-11-45-52-utc-300x200.jpg) Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the power requirements of modern data centers. At this point in the timeline of AI’s continued evolution, this statement should not be controversial. The deployment of increasingly large GPU clusters for training and inference purposes, such as [NVIDIA’s 72-GPU Vera Rubin model](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-rubin-nvl72/), is causing rack power densities to climb from tens to hundreds of kilowatts (kW), with some next-generation designs projected to exceed one megawatt (MW) per rack. This creates much more power demand than traditional enterprise computing infrastructure was designed to support. Workloads that behave very differently than conventional applications are forcing operators to reevaluate their long-standing assumptions about power delivery and efficiency. Infra & Chips.content: [![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/original/3d29ee764468946010cfa143e7c78b54:5d0164ae187a91ef56d93fd8ff9f0c71/ai-magazine-light-logo.png)](/ "Home") Article AI Applications # SambaNova Systems: Fast AI Inference Chips at US$11bn Value By[Diya Joseph](/author/diya-joseph) October 23, 2026 undefined mins Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google ![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/138/11b8f11fda84be7753c9fc18d62126db:0727cad3a90b5bc05fe68f06ee024d07/purchased-from-silicon-valley-business-journal.webp) Co-Founders Kunle Olukotun, Christopher Ré and Rodrigo Liang established SambaNova Systems to innovate AI hardware technology. Credit: SambaNova Systems SambaNova Systems Co-Founder and CEO Rodrigo Liang is betting on fast AI inference chips for agentic AI, with Intel, SoftBank and JPMorganChase on board In early 2026, takeover talks between [SambaNova Systems](https://aimagazine.com/company/sambanova-systems) and Intel had hit a standstill. Six months later, SambaNova emerged with an US$11bn valuation, backed by Intel as a strategic partner and investor rather than an owner. This turnaround highlights where the AI chip market is heading. While training giant models made NVIDIA the world’s most me-valued chipmaker, running those models for millions of users presents a different challenge. Speed and cost per token now decide which company wins. Consequently, SambaNova has pivoted towards the inference market. Its new SN50 chip is pitched squarely at the agentic AI era. > SambaNova’s US$11bn valuation highlights the central role that fast inference now plays in the enterprise AI stack > > Rodrigo Liang, Co-Founder and CEO at SambaNova Systems ## What is SambaNova’s tech ecosystem? Founded in 2017 and based in San Jose, US, SambaNova designs its own processors, which it terms Reconfigurable Dataflow Units. Rather than selling chips in isolation, the company packages them into full systems and services. These services include SambaCloud for developers and SambaStack and SambaManaged for operators who want to run their own inference clouds. It also offers SambaRack hardware for on-premises deployment. The SN50, unveiled in February 2026, serves as the centrepiece of this technology ecosystem. SambaNova claims it runs up to five times faster than competing chips at up to three times lower total cost of ownership. The chip links up to 256 accelerators and supports models with more than 10 trillion parameters. These performance figures have helped the business win serious customers across multiple sectors. [Rodrigo Liang](https://aimagazine.com/executive/rodrigo-liang), Co-Founder and CEO at SambaNova Systems, says: “SambaNova’s US$11bn valuation highlights the central role that fast inference now plays in the enterprise AI stack.” Rodrigo Liang, Co-Founder and CEO at SambaNova Systems. Credit: Rodrigo Liang/LinkedIn ## Enterprise clients deploying SambaNova hardware JPMorganChase selected SambaNova as an inference infrastructure partner and is deploying SN40 and SN50 systems on premises. SoftBank Corp. will be the first company to deploy the SN50 in its next-generation data centres in Japan. In addition, TEPCO Systems will distribute the technology across Japan’s power sector. In Europe, OVHcloud and Infercom have built inference services on SambaNova hardware. The relationship with Intel has evolved into a strategic partnership rather than a corporate acquisition. A multi-year collaboration covers an Intel Xeon-based AI cloud and joint selling initiatives across global markets. It also includes a blueprint for heterogeneous inference that uses GPUs for prefill, SambaNova chips for decode and Xeon 6 processors for agentic tools. Intel Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan also chairs SambaNova’s board. Infra & Chips.content: [Skip to content](#main) [Global](https://www.citybiz.co/city/global/), [San Francisco](https://www.citybiz.co/city/san-francisco/) [General Business](https://www.citybiz.co/channel/general-business/), [Internet / Technology](https://www.citybiz.co/channel/internet-technology/), [People](https://www.citybiz.co/channel/people/) # Infinity Appoints Aditya Om and Elliot Arledge to Expand AI Chip Inference Optimization October 23, 2026 ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Aditya-Om-and-Elliot-Arledge.jpg) Aditya Om and Elliot Arledge **Infinity**, a San Francisco-based automated AI research company, has appointed **Aditya Om** as Staff Inference Optimization Engineer and **Elliot Arledge** as Member of Technical Staff as it expands development of software designed to accelerate AI inference on specialized chips. Om joins Infinity from Meta Superintelligence Labs, where he worked on software infrastructure for the company’s internal AI training and inference chips. Arledge brings expertise in CUDA programming and GPU optimization, having developed educational courses on large language models and compute kernels that have reached more than two million learners. The appointments support Infinity’s development of Ignition, an autonomous AI research agent designed to generate, test and optimize the low-level software required to run AI models efficiently on different chip architectures. “We’re hiring engineers to solve the greatest engineering challenges of our generation,” said **Jeremy Nixon**, Founder and CEO of Infinity. Nixon said the company’s objective is to automate the development of inference software, reducing the time required to prepare new AI chips for running advanced models. Before joining Meta, Om worked at Lightmatter, where he developed collective communications software for the company’s Passage platform. He also contributed to research on Lightmatter’s Envise technology published in Nature and previously worked as an Internet of Things systems design engineer at Intel. Om holds a master’s degree in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor. Arledge, a self-taught CUDA and kernel engineer, has developed courses focused on training large language models and optimizing GPU compute operations. At Infinity, he will contribute to the company’s automated AI infrastructure development efforts. Infinity’s Ignition platform is designed to address a challenge facing emerging AI chip manufacturers: developing the software infrastructure needed to support competitive inference performance. While established chip platforms benefit from extensive software ecosystems, newer hardware architectures often require substantial engineering work to optimize AI models for production deployment. Infinity aims to automate portions of that process through AI agents that write, test and refine compute kernels based on hardware performance feedback. In a previously published case study involving chip developer d-Matrix, Infinity reported achieving 92% of a chip’s theoretical peak performance within 10 hours of initial hardware access. The company also reported running three frontier AI models end-to-end within 10 days. Infinity maintains a design partnership with d-Matrix, whose Corsair chip supports inference workloads through the Infinity d-Matrix Cloud. The company has also announced a collaboration with HP Inc. to optimize NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Super model on the HP ZGX Fury platform, powered by the NVIDIA GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip. Founded in August 2025 by Nixon, a former Google Brain researcher and co-founder of AGI House, Infinity is backed by Touring Capital and angel investors with backgrounds in AI research and semiconductor technology.
